full_judgment: 11. Admittedly the added respondent-opposite party No. I was not a party to the suit nor a party to the agreement and he is not a necessary party to the suit. In this connection a reference may be made to the case of Nitai Ch. Shaha vs. M/S City Ice and Cold Storage Ltd. & ors. reported In 35 D.L.R 60 wherein a Division Bench of this Court took a similar view. Mr. Quayum has drawn my attention to the case of Bajrang Lal Agarwala vs. Aksed Ali Shaikh & others reported in 35 D.L.R. 110, wherein it was held that in order to make an effective and complete adjudication in the matter in dispute and avoidance of further litigation a party may be added in a suit for specific performance of contract. In that case the order was passed in the suit itself. Mr. Quayum also cited the case of Sarada Kanta Das vs. Gobinda Mohan Da; reported in 6 Indian Cases at page 912, wherein a party was added as respondent. In that case the case was originated from a probate proceeding and it was held that the appellate Court has inherent power to add respondent who was not a party in the original Court. There is no hard and fast rule that no party can be added in a suit for specific performance of contract and in appeal, but law has put certain limitation and every case should be considered on its own merit. In the instant case the plaintiff prayed for a decree for specific performance of contract against the defendant-opposite party Nos. 5-7 who are entreting parties and added other defendants who are lessess of the suit land as in the mean time the suit property was declared as vested property. It was up to the plaintiff to add any other person he bethought fit and he did not implead the opposite party No. 1 and no relief was claimed against him. But before the appellate Court he himself filed an application to be added as a party. The appellate Court in a fit case has jurisdiction to add any person as defendant if his presence is necessary in order to dispose of the dispute effectively and completely. The power of addition by the appellate Court is sparingly used in exceptional cases for the ends of justice. In the instant case the learned Subordinate Judge did not come to any finding as to whether the addition of the opposite party No. 1 was necessary for effective and complete adjudication of the matter in dispute. He passed the order as if it is a routine work. All orders are not liable to be inerfered with under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If the order suffers from any error of law occasioning failure of justice only in that case the order is interfered with. In the instant case addition of opposite party No. 1 in the appellate stage will create an anamolous position. He was not a party to the suit and naturally did not file any written statement and if he is allowed to contest in the appeal he will have to file written statement in the suit resulting in fresh hearing of the suit. Even the plaintiff will have to face a party against whom no relief is prayed for and in a matter not connected with the contract in question, apart from necessity in disposal of the matter. So the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law by allowing the opposite party No. 1 to be added as a respondent occasioning failure of justice and as such interference of this Court under section 115 C.P.C. is called for.
